newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf states find supporting U.S. attack difficult.
newsitem.headline: Gulf states find supporting U.S. attack difficult.

text.p: Some Gulf Arab states will find it difficult to support cruise missile attacks against their Gulf War enemy Iraq by the their main ally the United States, analysts in the region said on Tuesday.
"It is difficult to justify this attack to our peoples," said one, stressing that "ordinary Gulf citizens are surprised and there is no justification for the attack".

Early on Tuesday the United States fired 27 missiles at air defence targets in southern Iraq in retaliation for Baghdad's military intervention on Saturday on the side of one Kurdish group against a rival faction in northern Iraq.

But diplomats and Gulf sources said the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states were eager not to appear as playing any role in the military strikes and some have even expressed to Washington their opposition to the move.
"America can't really intervene in this Kurdish issue, appearing to side with one Kurdish group, which is backed by Iran, against Iraq-supported Kurds," said one analyst.
The Arab League, of which all GCC states are members, on Tuesday condemned the U.S. attack on Iraq as infringing the sovereignty of an Arab country.
There are some 20,000 U.S. troops and 300 warplanes deployed in and around the Gulf, with some forces and aircraft based in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
It was not immediately clear if the GCC, which fought alongside the United States against Iraq in the 1991 war, would issue a joint statement similar to the League's condemnation.

Gulf analysts said some of those opposed to the strikes might fall short of openly criticising their key ally, the only Western power in the eyes of many GCC states capable of defending them in case of threats by their much larger neighbours Iraq and non-Arab Iran.
"But keeping silent means approval...They can't afford to appear in discord with their main ally," said a well-placed Gulf Arab source.

The GCC's dominant power and Washington's main Arab ally Riyadh has so far remained silent. Twenty-four Americans and two Indians were killed in two separate attacks on U.S. military complexes in the kingdom in November and June.
The GCC also groups Oman, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. Kuwait is the only GCC state so far to comment, saying it "fully understood" the U.S. attack.
But Kuwaitis were happy with the attack and said they wanted to see President Saddam Hussein toppled instead of hearing about one-off strikes against their former occupier.
"Stalling does not pay. I wish there were many more (strikes) to remove Saddam once and for all," Mariam al-Wagayan, a Kuwaiti civil servant, said.

Military experts said the missiles most probably hit targets of value like key command, control and communications (C3) centres and military installations rather than striking directly against Iraqi troops and their Kurdish allies involved in the fighting that started on Saturday in the north.

Several Gulf sources said the Kurdish fighting was a more complicated issue than Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, stressing that Washington was ignoring the various elements of the dispute including Iran's reported arming of one faction.
Iran has denied any role in the dispute.
"We don't see an Iraqi violation of U.N. resolutions here. It is an internal issue and Iraq's sovereignty has been threatened by others like Iran's role in the dispute," one Gulf source said.

In a reflection of what diplomats said was official UAE thinking, the semi-official al-Ittihad daily on Monday said President Saddam Hussein's incursion into northern Iraq was an attempt to unite his country and enjoyed wide Kurdish support.
Diplomats said the editorial portrayed the UAE's view that the fighting was Iraq's response to repeated violations of its territory by Iran and Turkey.
They said it also expressed the UAE's opposition ahead of the strikes, regarding Iraq's intervention an internal issue within Baghdad's right to defend national sovereignty.
